title: Foundations: Workplace Romance - The Complete Guide
summary: What Workplace Romance books are, where the genre came from, and how to read them.
body:
Workplace Romance: Romance is the literature of the heart: courtship, misunderstanding, and the earned happy ending. Austen invented the modern form; every love story since negotiates with her.

History: Jane Austen's six novels (1811-1817) created the comedy-of-manners romance. The Brontes added passion; Georgette Heyer (1920s) invented the Regency romance; the modern romance industry descends from all three.

HOW TO READ THIS SHELF: start with the landmark titles below — each record carries the complete plot, themes, a quoted passage, and craft notes. Read foundations first, then follow the ladder: compounded titles deepen the form, advanced titles challenge it.

# Workplace Romance foundations: reading-plan calculator
def reading_plan(total_pages, pages_per_day, days_per_week=7):
    days = total_pages / pages_per_day
    weeks = days / days_per_week
    return days, weeks

def session_words(words_per_minute=250, minutes=30):
    return words_per_minute * minutes

for pages in [200, 300, 400]:
    d, w = reading_plan(pages, 30)
    print(f'{pages} pages at 30/day: {d:.0f} days (~{w:.1f} weeks)')
print('30-min session at 250 wpm:', session_words(), 'words')
program.note: Estimates reading schedules from page counts and pace.

title: Wuthering Heights (1847) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Wuthering Heights by Emily Bronte (1847): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Wuthering Heights by Emily Bronte (1847). Shelf fit: Love as a force of nature.

COMPLETE PLOT: Heathcliff and Catherine's feral childhood bond curdles when she marries Edgar Linton; Heathcliff's revenge consumes two generations until the second Catherine and Hareton break the cycle. The moors themselves seem to love and hate.

THEMES: Love as destruction and transcendence.

FROM THE TEXT: "Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same."

CRAFT NOTE: Bronte's nested narrators (Lockwood, Nelly) keep the passion at one remove - unbearable otherwise.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: Love as a force of nature. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Emma (1815) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Emma by Jane Austen (1815): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Emma by Jane Austen (1815). Shelf fit: The matchmaker who cannot see herself.

COMPLETE PLOT: Emma Woodhouse schemes to marry off Harriet Smith, misreads every heart including her own, and is gently educated by Mr. Knightley - the only person who tells her the truth - into self-knowledge and love.

THEMES: Self-deception vs. self-knowledge.

FROM THE TEXT: "If I loved you less, I might be able to talk about it more."

CRAFT NOTE: Austen's most perfect comedy: the heroine is the obstacle.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: The matchmaker who cannot see herself. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: North and South (1855) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for North and South by Elizabeth Gaskell (1855): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
North and South by Elizabeth Gaskell (1855). Shelf fit: Industrial England's love story.

COMPLETE PLOT: Margaret Hale moves from the south to Milton, clashes with mill owner John Thornton over workers' rights, and slowly recognizes his honor - as he recognizes hers. The strike, the riot, and the union chapters braid romance with social reform.

THEMES: Love across the class divide; principle tested by feeling.

FROM THE TEXT: "Gaskell's question: can principle and feeling both be right?"

CRAFT NOTE: Gaskell makes the romance carry the Condition-of-England novel.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: Industrial England's love story. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

body:
Anne of Green Gables by L. M. Montgomery (1908). Shelf fit: The slow-burn childhood sweethearts.

COMPLETE PLOT: Orphan Anne Shirley comes to Green Gables, feuds with Gilbert Blythe after he calls her 'Carrots,' and over years of rivalry and friendship falls in love with him - sealed when he gives up the Avonlea school so she can stay with Marilla.

THEMES: Rivalry ripening into love; imagination as survival.

FROM THE TEXT: "Isn't it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?"

CRAFT NOTE: Montgomery's slow burn: the romance earns every page.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: The slow-burn childhood sweethearts. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Little Women (1868) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Little Women by Louisa May Alcott (1868): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Little Women by Louisa May Alcott (1868). Shelf fit: Sisterhood and suitors.

COMPLETE PLOT: The March sisters come of age during the Civil War: Meg marries Brooke, Jo refuses Laurie (the era's great romantic swerve) and eventually marries Professor Bhaer, Amy marries Laurie, Beth dies. Love here is one thread among family, work, and art.

THEMES: Love vs. vocation; the family as the real romance.

FROM THE TEXT: "I want to do something splendid before I go into my castle."

CRAFT NOTE: Alcott refuses the easy pairing - Jo's choice is the novel's revolution.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: Sisterhood and suitors. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett (1911): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett (1911). Shelf fit: Love of the living world.

COMPLETE PLOT: Spoiled Mary Lennox and sickly Colin Craven heal each other through a hidden garden at Misselthwaite - with Dickon, who charms animals, as their guide. The garden's revival mirrors the children's.

THEMES: Nature as healer; chosen family.

FROM THE TEXT: "If you look the right way, you can see that the whole world is a garden."

CRAFT NOTE: Burnett's romance is with life itself - the garden as love object.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: Love of the living world. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for Persuasion by Jane Austen (1817): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Persuasion by Jane Austen (1817). Shelf fit: The second-chance masterpiece.

COMPLETE PLOT: Anne Elliot refused Captain Wentworth at nineteen on Lady Russell's advice; eight years later he returns rich and admired, and Anne must win back the man she lost - culminating in his letter: 'You pierce my soul.'

THEMES: Constancy vs. prudence; love's second chance.

FROM THE TEXT: "You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope."

CRAFT NOTE: Austen's most moving romance: the happy ending is earned by waiting.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: The second-chance masterpiece. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for Far from the Madding Crowd by Thomas Hardy (1874): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Far from the Madding Crowd by Thomas Hardy (1874). Shelf fit: Love among the sheep farms.

COMPLETE PLOT: Bathsheba Everdene rejects steady Gabriel Oak, marries dashing Sergeant Troy, is widowed by his apparent drowning, and finally - after Troy's murder by the obsessed Boldwood - marries Oak, who waited and worked.

THEMES: Steadfastness vs. glamour.

FROM THE TEXT: "Hardy's Wessex: love measured in seasons, not weeks."

CRAFT NOTE: Hardy's Wessex makes the romance geological - slow, deep, inevitable.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: Love among the sheep farms. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

A Room with a View by E. M. Forster (1908). Shelf fit: Italy vs. England in the heart.

COMPLETE PLOT: Lucy Honeychurch is kissed by George Emerson in a Florentine violet field, flees back to English propriety and Cecil Vyse, then breaks free - with Mr. Emerson senior's plain wisdom - to choose George and passion.

THEMES: Passion vs. propriety; Italy as liberation.

FROM THE TEXT: "Forster's Italy: where the heart learns to speak."

CRAFT NOTE: Forster's comedy of manners with a beating heart.

Pollyanna by Eleanor H. Porter (1913). Shelf fit: The glad game as romance with life.

FROM THE TEXT: "When you look for the bad, expecting it, you will get it."

CRAFT NOTE: Porter's structure: one girl's game reorganizes every relationship in town.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: The glad game as romance with life. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Pride and Prejudice (1813) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen (1813): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen (1813). Shelf fit: The romance all romances answer to.

COMPLETE PLOT: Elizabeth Bennet spars with the proud Mr. Darcy, rejects his first proposal, then rereads his letter of explanation, sees her own prejudice, and accepts him when both have changed. Wickham's elopement with Lydia forces the crisis; Darcy's secret rescue proves his love.

THEMES: Pride, prejudice, and moral growth; love as recognition.

FROM THE TEXT: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife."

CRAFT NOTE: Austen's free indirect style lets us live inside Elizabeth's misjudgments - romance as moral education.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: The romance all romances answer to. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The romance all romances answer to.
Themes: Pride, prejudice, and moral growth; love as recognition.

title: Jane Eyre (1847) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte (1847): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte (1847). Shelf fit: Passion with a conscience.

COMPLETE PLOT: Orphaned Jane becomes governess at Thornfield, falls in love with the brooding Rochester - and flees on her wedding day when his wife Bertha is revealed in the attic. Independent at last, she returns to a blinded Rochester as his equal.

THEMES: Integrity vs. passion; the heroine who will not be kept.

FROM THE TEXT: "Reader, I married him."

CRAFT NOTE: Bronte's first-person intensity makes Jane's moral choice the climax, not the wedding.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE WORKPLACE ROMANCE SHELF: Passion with a conscience. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: Passion with a conscience.
Themes: Integrity vs. passion; the heroine who will not be kept.
